title: Adult basic life support and in-hospital cardiac arrest
blurb: Recognise cardiac arrest, call for help, give high-quality CPR and use an AED to RCUK 2025 standards, in the community and in hospital.
question: Mr Ahmed, 67, is found on a ward unresponsive in bed, making occasional gasping breaths. According to RCUK 2025 guidance, what should the nurse do?

teach.body: Cardiac arrest is the sudden loss of effective heart function, so the person becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally. Survival depends on early recognition, calling for help, prompt high-quality CPR and early defibrillation; bystander CPR and AED use increase survival two to four-fold. The RCUK 2025 change: call 999 for anyone who is unresponsive, then assess breathing while waiting for the call to be answered. Plain English: if they will not wake, call first.
teach.cite: RCUK 2025 Adult basic life support guidelines (27 October 2025)

teach.h: Outside hospital: 3 steps to save a life

steps.label: Check
steps.sub: Is it safe? Is the person conscious?

steps.label: Assess breathing
steps.sub: While the call connects; the call handler helps

steps.label: AED
steps.sub: Attach as soon as available; follow prompts

teach.caption: Alone without a phone signal: shout for help and assess breathing; if no one will come, leave to call 999 as quickly as possible.

teach.body: Slow, laboured breathing, agonal gasping and even panting must be recognised as signs of cardiac arrest; athletes may show near-normal or panting breaths early on. A short period of seizure-like activity can happen at the onset: once it stops, assess breathing. If anyone is unresponsive with abnormal breathing, assume cardiac arrest. If in any doubt, start CPR: the risk of harm from CPR to someone not in arrest is low.

items.label: of the sternum, heel of hand
depth: at least 5, no more than 6

teach.caption: Let the chest recoil fully after each compression and keep interruptions to a minimum.

items: Heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum, other hand on top, fingers interlocked, arms straight, shoulders vertically above the chest.
Do not move someone from a bed to the floor: start CPR on the bed and compress deeper if the mattress is soft.
Rescue breaths: just enough air to make the chest start to rise; avoid over-ventilation. If two attempts fail, consider choking.
Not trained in rescue breaths? Give continuous chest compressions without interruptions.

steps.label: Pads on bare chest
steps.sub: As pictured; CPR continues while pads go on

steps.label: Restart CPR at once
steps.sub: After a shock, or if no shock is advised

teach.caption: A bra can stay if the pads can be placed correctly on bare skin; remove it if it gets in the way. Anyone can use an AED.

teach.h: In hospital: collapsed or sick patient (RCUK 2025)

root.label: Shout for help and assess
root.sub: Signs of life? Responsive, breathing normally

children.label: Cardiac arrest: Call, Compress, Collect
children.sub: 2222; CPR with oxygen and airway adjuncts; pads; defibrillate if indicated

children.label: Medical emergency: ABCDE
children.sub: High-flow oxygen, monitoring, IV access; call team if needed

teach.caption: Switch compressors at every rhythm assessment. Hand over to the resuscitation team when they arrive.

teach.h: In-hospital timing to be aware of (RCUK 2025 ALS)
head: Item
Standard
rows: 1 mg IV as soon as possible
1 mg IV after the third shock
300 mg after 3 shocks; 150 mg after 5 shocks
teach.caption: Drug decisions belong to the ALS team; nurses need to know the timings to prepare and record. Hospitals use track-and-trigger scores and let patients and families request urgent review to prevent arrests.

teach.h: Worked example: Mr Ahmed on a medical ward
items: The nurse finds him unresponsive with occasional gasps: agonal breathing means cardiac arrest. She shouts for help and presses the emergency buzzer.
A colleague calls 2222 and brings the resuscitation trolley and defibrillator; the nurse lays the bed flat and starts compressions on the bed at 100–120 per minute, 5–6 cm deep.
A second colleague gives breaths by bag-mask with oxygen, 30:2. Pads go on while compressions continue.
At each rhythm assessment the compressor changes. The resuscitation team arrives and the nurse hands over using a brief structured summary, then records times and actions.

teach.text: The 2025 sequence is call first, then assess breathing: you no longer need to confirm abnormal breathing before calling 999. Gasping is not breathing. And never drag someone from a bed to the floor to start CPR.

items: Unresponsive: call 999 (or 2222 in hospital) first, then assess breathing.
Unresponsive with abnormal breathing, including gasping: cardiac arrest; if in doubt, start CPR.
Lower half of sternum, 5–6 cm, 100–120 per minute, full recoil, 30:2 if trained.
AED as soon as available; nobody touches during analysis or shock; restart CPR immediately.
Hospital: Call, Compress, Collect; defibrillate within 3 minutes; switch compressor at each rhythm check.

summary: You can now recognise cardiac arrest, including agonal or abnormal breathing, call for help in the right order and deliver high-quality CPR with early AED use to RCUK 2025 standards. You know the in-hospital response and the key timings for defibrillation and adrenaline.

A.q: According to RCUK 2025, where should the hands be placed for adult chest compressions?
options: On the upper half of the sternum
Over the left side of the chest
On the lower half of the sternum
Over the xiphoid process
A.why: RCUK 2025: place the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum ('in the centre of the chest'), with the other hand on top.

whyNot.0: The upper sternum is too high to compress the heart effectively.
whyNot.1: Compressing over the left chest risks rib fractures and is less effective.
whyNot.3: Pressing on the xiphoid process is below the correct position and risks injury.

A.q: A trained nurse is giving rescue breaths during CPR. How much air should each breath deliver?
options: Enough to inflate the chest fully
Just enough to make the chest start to rise
As much air as she can blow in
A slow breath lasting about 5 seconds
A.why: RCUK 2025: deliver just enough air to make the chest start to rise, avoiding excessive ventilation.

whyNot.0: Full inflation means over-ventilation, which RCUK advises against.
whyNot.2: Maximal breaths over-ventilate and can inflate the stomach.
whyNot.3: A 5-second breath prolongs interruptions to compressions.

A.q: A visitor who is not trained in rescue breaths begins CPR on a man who collapsed in a hospital car park. What should he do?
options: 30 compressions, then pause for 10 seconds
Rescue breaths every 6 seconds, no compressions
15 compressions to 2 rescue breaths
Continuous chest compressions without pauses
A.why: RCUK 2025: if not trained to provide rescue breaths, perform continuous chest compressions without interruptions.

whyNot.0: Regular pauses reduce blood flow; untrained rescuers keep compressing.
whyNot.1: Compressions are the priority; breaths without compressions do not circulate blood.
whyNot.2: 15:2 is not the adult ratio, and he is not trained in breaths.

B.q: Mr Daly, 59, suddenly collapses in a clinic waiting room. His limbs jerk for about 20 seconds; he then stays unresponsive with slow gasping breaths. What should the nurse do?
options: Call for help and start CPR
Recovery position, as this was a seizure
Wait 5 minutes for him to come round
Cushion his head and keep observing
B.why: RCUK 2025: a short period of seizure-like activity may occur at the onset of cardiac arrest. Once it stops, an unresponsive person with abnormal breathing is in cardiac arrest: call for help and start CPR.

whyNot.1: Gasping is abnormal breathing; the recovery position is for people breathing normally.
whyNot.2: Waiting wastes the minutes in which CPR and defibrillation save lives.
whyNot.3: Observing an unresponsive, gasping person delays life-saving CPR.

B.q: An AED arrives during CPR on Mrs Bond, 62, who is wearing a bra. What does RCUK 2025 advise?
options: Place the pads over the bra to save time
Wait for a female colleague to apply the pads
Cut the bra off before switching on the AED
Leave it if the pads can sit correctly on bare skin
B.why: RCUK 2025: prioritise correct pad placement on bare skin. If this can be achieved quickly with the bra in place, it can stay; if it interferes, remove it. Rescuers should not hesitate to expose the chest.

whyNot.0: Pads must be in contact with bare skin.
whyNot.1: Delaying defibrillation for this reason is unsafe; life-saving care comes first.
whyNot.2: Removal is needed when the bra interferes, but switching on and pad placement should not be delayed.

B.q: A nurse finds Mrs Grant, 81, in a side room with no signs of life. Under the RCUK 2025 in-hospital algorithm, what are her first actions?
options: Call for help and the team, start CPR, get equipment
Fetch the defibrillator before calling anyone
Complete a full ABCDE before calling the team
Give rescue breaths for 1 minute, then call
B.why: RCUK 2025 in-hospital algorithm: in cardiac arrest, Call, Compress, Collect: call the resuscitation team (2222), start CPR, collect equipment, with tasks done at the same time if staff are available.

whyNot.1: Leaving without calling for help or starting CPR delays both.
whyNot.2: ABCDE is for patients with signs of life; she has none.
whyNot.3: Breaths without compressions and a delayed call are not the algorithm.

C.q: During an in-hospital cardiac arrest on a ward, when should the person doing chest compressions be changed, according to the RCUK 2025 algorithm?
options: After each adrenaline dose
At every rhythm assessment
Every 10 minutes of CPR
When the team leader arrives
C.why: RCUK 2025 in-hospital algorithm: switch compressor at every rhythm assessment, to keep compressions effective with minimal interruption.

whyNot.0: Adrenaline timing is every 3–5 minutes and is not the cue for swapping.
whyNot.2: Ten minutes is far too long; fatigue reduces compression quality.
whyNot.3: The arrival of the team leader is not the RCUK cue to change compressor.

C.q: Mr Fox, 70, is in ventricular fibrillation on a coronary care unit. The ALS team is defibrillating. When is the first dose of adrenaline given?
options: Before the first shock
After the first shock
After the third shock
After the fifth shock
C.why: RCUK 2025 ALS: for shockable rhythms give adrenaline 1 mg IV after the third shock, then every 3–5 minutes; amiodarone 300 mg is also given after 3 shocks.

whyNot.0: Defibrillation comes first in shockable rhythms; adrenaline is not given before shocks.
whyNot.1: After the first shock, CPR continues; adrenaline waits until after the third.
whyNot.3: After the fifth shock is when the second amiodarone dose (150 mg) is considered, not the first adrenaline.

C.q: Mrs Lowe, 75, collapses in a ward bay. She is drowsy but breathing normally and has a pulse. Under the RCUK 2025 in-hospital algorithm, what should the nurse do?
options: Start CPR as a precaution until the team arrives
Leave her to fetch the defibrillator first
Recovery position and recheck in 30 minutes
ABCDE assessment with high-flow oxygen and monitoring
C.why: RCUK 2025: if there are signs of life this is a medical emergency: call and collect, ABCDE assessment, high-flow oxygen (titrated to SpO2), monitoring and IV access, and call the team if needed.

whyNot.0: CPR is for people without signs of life; she has a pulse and normal breathing.
whyNot.1: Leaving her alone delays assessment of a medical emergency.
whyNot.2: A 30-minute wait is unsafe after a collapse; she needs ABCDE now.

reteach.title: Call first, push hard, push fast
reteach.question: If you remember only three things in an emergency, what should they be?

blocks.body: Call: anyone unresponsive gets a 999 or 2222 call straight away. Push: if they are not breathing normally, start compressions on the lower half of the sternum, 5–6 cm deep, 100–120 a minute. Shock: get the AED on as soon as it arrives and do what it says. Everything else supports these three.

blocks.text: Gasping, slow or laboured breathing is abnormal breathing: treat it as cardiac arrest, not as a sign of life.

explain.body: Unresponsive with abnormal breathing: slow, laboured, agonal gasping or panting. Brief seizure-like activity may occur at onset. If in doubt, start CPR.

test.q: Which breathing pattern in an unresponsive adult should be treated as cardiac arrest?
options: Regular breaths at 16 per minute
Quiet, even snoring with good colour
Occasional gasping breaths
Normal breathing after a faint
test.why: RCUK 2025: agonal gasping, slow or laboured breathing are signs of cardiac arrest.

whyNot.0: Regular breathing at a normal rate is normal breathing.
whyNot.1: Even breathing with good colour suggests the person is breathing, though the airway needs attention.
whyNot.3: Normal breathing after a faint is not cardiac arrest.

explain.body: Lower half of the sternum, 5–6 cm deep, 100–120 per minute, full recoil without leaning, minimal interruptions.

test.q: What should happen between each chest compression?
options: The chest recoils fully, without leaning
Pressure is held for 1 second
The rescuer checks for a pulse
The hands lift well off the chest
test.why: RCUK 2025: allow the chest to recoil completely after each compression and avoid leaning on the chest.

whyNot.1: Holding pressure reduces the rate and the refill of the heart.
whyNot.2: Pulse checks between compressions cause harmful interruptions.
whyNot.3: Lifting the hands off risks losing the correct position; recoil needs no lift-off.

explain.body: Switch on, follow prompts, pads on bare chest while CPR continues, nobody touching during analysis or shock, restart compressions immediately afterwards.

test.q: An AED has just delivered a shock. What should rescuers do next?
options: Check for a pulse for 10 seconds
Restart chest compressions straight away
Wait for the AED to reanalyse
Place the person in the recovery position
test.why: RCUK 2025: after the shock has been delivered, immediately restart chest compressions and continue to follow the AED instructions.

whyNot.0: A pulse check delays compressions; the AED will prompt the next analysis.
whyNot.2: Reanalysis comes after a period of CPR, not straight after the shock.
whyNot.3: The recovery position is not used unless there are clear signs of life and normal breathing.

explain.body: 2222 for the arrest team; Call, Compress, Collect; CPR with oxygen and airway adjuncts; defibrillate within 3 minutes for shockable rhythms; adrenaline as soon as possible for non-shockable rhythms.

test.q: RCUK 2025 says hospitals should aim to defibrillate shockable rhythms within what time?
options: 3 minutes
10 minutes
5 minutes
1 hour
test.why: RCUK 2025 ALS: hospital systems should aim to defibrillate rapidly, in under 3 minutes, for shockable rhythms.

whyNot.1: Ten minutes would greatly reduce the chance of survival.
whyNot.2: Five minutes is longer than the RCUK target.
whyNot.3: An hour is far beyond any resuscitation standard.
